proof_skeleton_nl: Rewrite the original summand exactly by the elementary identity ((q^d;q^d)_k)^2/(q^{2d};q^{2d})_k=(q^d;q^d)_k/(-q^d;q^d)_k, and clear the remaining normalized denominators by the common factor D_{d,n}(q). This produces a cleared Laurent polynomial H_{d,r,n}(q). The first substantive input is a strictly weaker lemma asserting that H_{d,r,n}(q) is divisible by [n]_q; write H_{d,r,n}(q)=[n]_q J(q). The second, more delicate input compares the quotient J(q) directly with the quotient of the claimed right-hand side, namely D_{d,n}(q) q^{r(1-n)/2} Σ_{j=0}^{r-1} q^{jn}, at primitive nth roots of unity up to first derivative. The abstract double-root lemma then upgrades this primitive-root comparison to divisibility of the quotient difference by Φ_n(q)^2. Multiplying back by [n]_q gives divisibility of D_{d,n}(q) times the theorem difference by [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2. Finally, coprimality of D_{d,n}(q) with the modulus allows cancellation in the localized congruence ring, yielding the original theorem exactly.

steps.derives: From the hypotheses n > 1 and n ≡ 1 mod 2d, conclude that n is odd and gcd(d,n)=1.
steps.trivial_justification: Writing n = 1 + 2dt for some integer t shows immediately that n is odd. Any common divisor of d and n also divides n-2dt = 1, so gcd(d,n)=1.

steps.derives: Define S(q) = Σ_{k=0}^{n-1} [3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k (q^d;q^d)_k^2 q^{k(d-dk-2r)/2} / (q^{2d};q^{2d})_k, define R(q) = [rn]_q q^{r(1-n)/2}, define D(q) = ∏_{k=0}^{n-1} (-q^d;q^d)_k, and define H(q) = D(q) · Σ_{k=0}^{n-1} [3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k (q^d;q^d)_k q^{k(d-dk-2r)/2} / (-q^d;q^d)_k. Then D(q)·S(q) = H(q), hence D(q)·(S(q)-R(q)) = H(q) - D(q)R(q).
steps.trivial_justification: Lemma L1 rewrites the factor ((q^d;q^d)_k)^2/(q^{2d};q^{2d})_k exactly as (q^d;q^d)_k/(-q^d;q^d)_k for each summand. Multiplying the normalized sum by D(q) therefore gives precisely H(q). Subtracting D(q)R(q) from both sides yields the identity for D(q)(S(q)-R(q)).

steps.derives: The cleared sum H(q) lies in the Laurent polynomial ring Z[q^{±1}].
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the content of Lemma L3 for the locally defined H(q).

steps.derives: There exists a Laurent polynomial J(q) in Z[q^{±1}] such that H(q) = [n]_q J(q).
steps.trivial_justification: Lemma L4 states that [n]_q divides H(q) in Z[q^{±1}]. By the definition of divisibility in that ring, a quotient J(q) exists with H(q) = [n]_q J(q).

steps.derives: If G(q) = Σ_{j=0}^{r-1} q^{jn}, then R(q) = [n]_q G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2}, and therefore D(q)R(q) = [n]_q D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2}.
steps.trivial_justification: Lemma L5 gives [rn]_q = [n]_q G(q). Substituting this into the definition R(q) = [rn]_q q^{r(1-n)/2} and multiplying by D(q) gives the displayed identity.
From A1, D(q)(S(q)-R(q)) = H(q)-D(q)R(q). Replace H(q) by [n]_q J(q) using A3, and replace D(q)R(q) by [n]_q D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2} using A4. Factoring out [n]_q gives the result.

steps.derives: For every primitive nth root of unity ζ, the two Laurent polynomials J(q) and B(q) = D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2} satisfy J(ζ) = B(ζ) and J'(ζ) = B'(ζ).
steps.trivial_justification: Lemma L7 applies exactly because A3 provides the required quotient identity H(q) = [n]_q J(q). Its conclusion is precisely the equality of values and first q-derivatives of J and B at every primitive nth root.

steps.derives: Φ_n(q)^2 divides J(q) - D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2} in Z[q^{±1}].
steps.trivial_justification: Apply Lemma L6 with A(q)=J(q) and B(q)=D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2}. Step A6 supplies exactly the hypotheses required by Lemma L6.

steps.derives: The modulus M(q) = [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2 divides D(q)·(S(q)-R(q)) in Z[q^{±1}]. Equivalently, D(q)S(q) ≡ D(q)R(q) mod M(q).
steps.trivial_justification: Step A7 gives Φ_n(q)^2 | (J(q)-D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2}). Multiplying by [n]_q shows M(q) divides [n]_q (J(q)-D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2}). Step A5 identifies this latter Laurent polynomial with D(q)(S(q)-R(q)). Hence M(q) divides D(q)(S(q)-R(q)), i.e. D(q)S(q) ≡ D(q)R(q) mod M(q).

steps.derives: Let [m]_q = (1−q^m)/(1−q), let (a;q)_k = ∏_{j=0}^{k−1} (1−aq^j), let (a,b,c;q)_k = (a;q)_k (b;q)_k (c;q)_k, and let Φ_n(q) be the nth cyclotomic polynomial. Prove that for positive integers d and r with gcd(d,r)=1 and r ≤ d, and for every integer n > 1 with n ≡ 1 mod 2d, we have Σ_{k=0}^{n−1} [3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k (q^d;q^d)_k^2 q^(k(d−dk−2r)/2) / (q^{2d};q^{2d})_k ≡ [rn]_q q^(r(1−n)/2) mod [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2.
steps.trivial_justification: By A0, the hypotheses of Lemma L2 are satisfied, so D(q) is coprime to M(q)=[n]_q Φ_n(q)^2. The same lemma also shows that every normalized denominator (-q^d;q^d)_k is coprime to M(q), so the normalized expression for S(q) from A1 has denominator coprime to M(q). The right-hand side R(q)=[rn]_q q^{r(1-n)/2} also has denominator coprime to M(q) because q is invertible modulo any polynomial M with M(0)=1, and here M(0)=1 since n>1 implies [n]_q and Φ_n(q) both have constant term 1. Step A8 gives D(q)S(q) ≡ D(q)R(q) mod M(q). Lemma L8 says that multiplication by a polynomial coprime to M(q) preserves and reflects congruence modulo M(q). Applying Lemma L8 with F(q)=S(q), G(q)=R(q), M(q)=[n]_q Φ_n(q)^2, and D(q)=D_{d,n}(q) therefore yields S(q) ≡ R(q) mod [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2. Writing out S(q) and R(q) gives exactly the theorem statement.
